sections.title: How to Play Krillion: the seven-prompt Daily Dive

blocks.text: Krillion is an open-answer daily trivia game: every player receives the same seven prompts, but there are no multiple-choice buttons to lean on. Each prompt gives us 25 seconds to type one response. A recognised answer earns a rarity tier and a fixed number of points; an answer that is common, outside the category, misspelled beyond recognition, or left too late can leave us near the surface. The run ends after prompt seven, when the score is converted into metres of dive depth.

blocks.alt: Krillion Daily Dive title screen listing seven daily questions and one dive a day
blocks.caption: The title screen states the full contract before the clock begins: seven questions, seven prompts, and one Daily Dive.

blocks.text: The rule that matters most: valid first, rare second

The game rewards uncommon answers, but rarity is never permission to bend the wording. If the prompt asks for a U.S. state beginning with A, our legal pool is Alabama, Alaska, and Arizona. Octopus is unusual, perfectly spelled, and still worth nothing because it is not a state. That sounds obvious when the timer is stopped; under a 25-second countdown, category drift is the most expensive beginner mistake.

We play the seven prompts as seven separate decisions. A poor first answer does not make the second prompt harder, and a Deep Cut does not buy extra time on the next screen. Resetting after every result is part of the rules in practice. The only information carried forward is the growing score and depth; the next category starts clean.

sections.title: Before Begin Descent: prepare the screen and keyboard

blocks.text: Begin Descent is the real commitment point. We do not press it while deciding between portrait and landscape, changing keyboard language, or opening display controls. A Daily Dive only takes a few minutes, yet the prompts arrive fast enough that a small setup problem can consume half a turn. On desktop, click once inside the game so the embedded player owns the focus. On a phone, check that the page is at a comfortable zoom and that the browser bar is not covering the lower controls.
A one-minute preflight that protects the run

items: Wait until the actual Krillion title screen appears; the site cover and Play Now button are not the game itself.
Choose normal view or Webpage Fullscreen before starting. The view changes presentation, not the questions or scoring.
Use the keyboard layout in which you can spell proper names quickly, and turn off aggressive autocorrection if it keeps rewriting uncommon words.
Put the device on a stable connection and close overlays that might steal focus.
Set aside roughly five uninterrupted minutes. Looking away for one notification can cost an entire prompt.

blocks.label: Start only when the first prompt can have your full attention
blocks.body: There is no strategic benefit in beginning early. The cleanest first move is to remove display and keyboard uncertainty while the timer is still absent.

sections.title: Read a Krillion prompt inside the 25-second clock

blocks.text: We read from the category outward. First identify the noun the game wants: country, character, product, animal, literary device, team, food, or event. Then collect every qualifier around it: a starting letter, date, speed, franchise, location, current or former status, technical versus culinary meaning, or an explicit exclusion. Only after that do we recall answers. Reversing this order makes the first familiar word feel correct before we have finished reading.

blocks.alt: Live Krillion prompt asking for a U.S. state beginning with A with timer and answer controls visible
blocks.caption: This prompt is a closed pool. Once we identify the noun and the initial-letter rule, searching outside Alabama, Alaska, and Arizona only wastes the clock.

blocks.text: The timing is a guardrail, not a rhythm game. A closed prompt should be answered sooner because its legal set is small. A broad prompt such as a food served on a stick may justify a few more seconds of recall. What never changes is the five-second commitment line: once the clock reaches it, a safe answer already in hand is worth more than another speculative memory search.

sections.title: Build a three-candidate shortlist for Krillion

blocks.text: The shortlist is the simplest way to prevent both bland answers and empty boxes. Candidate one is the automatic safe response. Candidate two moves one ring away from it. Candidate three is a second valid alternative, not an obscure fact we barely remember. For a theme-park chain, that might mean Six Flags first, Legoland second, and a regional chain third. For a fictional robot, the headline mascot may be first while a supporting character such as Rosie from The Jetsons becomes the stronger second choice.
Run four filters before choosing the rarest candidate

rows: Is it exactly the kind of thing requested?
It is related to the topic but belongs to another class
Does it meet every letter, era, place, status, or property?
Would an ordinary reference list it under this wording?
It relies on a nickname or explanation
Can we spell it before the clock closes?

blocks.text: After testing this routine, we found the middle candidate wins more often than the heroic third one. It is far enough from the first instinct to escape the largest crowd, but familiar enough to survive the category and spelling checks. Save the risky third candidate for prompts in a subject we genuinely know well. Specialist confidence is useful; vague familiarity is not.

blocks.label: The one-ring rule
blocks.body: Move one ring away from the obvious answer, not five. Supporting characters, former teams, secondary products, regional foods, and less-advertised examples often earn a better tier without becoming fragile.

sections.title: Submit cleanly and recover from Krillion answer rejection

blocks.text: Type the shortest standard form that clearly identifies the answer. Explanations do not add rarity and can make matching harder. Watch the field on mobile because autocorrect may replace a proper noun after we have visually moved on. Then use the on-screen Dive control or the supported keyboard submission and look at the game’s response, not merely the fact that a key was pressed.

blocks.alt: Krillion displaying a not-on-this-answer-list warning while time remains
blocks.caption: The orange rejection message is gameplay feedback, not a frozen player. The running clock is the signal to replace the entry immediately.

blocks.text: Decide whether the problem is wording or category

A rejected proper name can sometimes be repaired with its standard full form, but a category error needs a different answer. The screenshot shows octopus entered for a state prompt. Changing punctuation or resubmitting OCTOPUS cannot help. The correct recovery is to erase it and use Alabama, Alaska, or Arizona while time remains. The shortlist matters here because the backup was chosen before the error appeared.

blocks.text: A recorded Sunday Wildcard run is useful because it contains ordinary decisions rather than seven perfect answers. The player begins with a Google product, avoids Gmail and Sheets, tries Google Ads, and receives a modest result. On an animal above 40 miles per hour, falcon is valid but not rare. The grain prompt finally produces the stronger buckwheat answer and a Rare result worth 60 points. That sequence shows why a run must be judged across all seven prompts: two common answers do not prevent a later good retrieval.

columns: Better lesson than memorising the answer

blocks.text: The player also demonstrates a sound emergency habit on the theme-park prompt: when a less obvious chain will not come back in time, Six Flags is typed and submitted near the deadline. It earns only ten points, but it keeps the run complete. On a later review screen, Legoland appears as a 30-point alternative. That comparison is actionable: next time, move one rung beyond the first chain only if the second name arrives cleanly.

What we would not copy is waiting until the last second as a standard tactic. It worked on Six Flags, but left no room for typo recovery or a rejected match. The run also shows that knowledge gaps are local. Not knowing supporting Avatar characters does not justify gambling on the next country prompt. Each new screen gets its own risk decision.

sections.title: Read Krillion results, ranks, and dive depth

blocks.text: Krillion uses six fixed visible tiers: Plankton is 10 points, Too Clever 15, Schooler 30, Rare 60, Deep Cut 85, and One in a Krillion 100. The final depth is the total score multiplied by ten. Seven Schooler answers make 210 points and 2,100 metres. A mixed run of 10 + 10 + 60 + 10 + 15 + 10 + 10 makes 125 points and 1,250 metres. The arithmetic is simple; the useful part is locating where points were lost.

blocks.text: For deeper score planning, use the dedicated scoring and rare-answer guide. For a blank player, missing keyboard focus, or mobile layout trouble, use the loading and input guide. Keeping those subjects separate matters: basic play is about making seven clean decisions, while score optimisation and browser recovery each need their own diagnostic tools.

items.question: How many prompts are in a Krillion Daily Dive?
items.answer: There are seven open-answer prompts. Each one is timed separately, and the final result combines the points from all seven.

items.question: How long do we have for each Krillion answer?
items.answer: The live prompt gives 25 seconds. Read the category first and treat five seconds remaining as the point to submit the safest valid candidate.

items.question: Do answers need to be complete sentences?
items.answer: No. Use the shortest conventional name that clearly matches the prompt. Extra explanation creates matching and typing risk without improving rarity.

items.question: Can we try again after Krillion rejects an answer?
items.answer: Yes when the rejection message appears and the clock is still moving. Replace the entry with the prepared fallback instead of repeating the same category mistake.

items.question: Should a beginner chase One in a Krillion every time?
items.answer: No. Complete all seven prompts first. Upgrade the obvious answer when a clearly valid alternative arrives quickly, and accept a safe response in weak categories.

items.question: What is the difference between Krillion score and depth?
items.answer: The six rarity tiers award points. At the end of the run, the point total is multiplied by ten to produce the displayed depth in metres.

blocks.title: Krillion | Sunday Wildcard September 13, 2026
blocks.summary: This 4:35 recording follows one Daily Dive from Begin Descent through all seven prompts and the post-run answer reveal. It is valuable because the run mixes a Rare result with several ordinary answers and shows how the player handles limited knowledge without abandoning the attempt.

segments.heading: Start, Google product, and fast-animal prompts
segments.text: The player begins immediately, rejects Gmail and Sheets as too obvious, then submits Google Ads. Falcon is the next safe answer. Both are valid examples of moving beyond the first thought without overcomplicating the entry.

segments.heading: Buckwheat earns the run's clear Rare result
segments.text: Rice and wheat are recognised as crowded, so buckwheat becomes the one-ring alternative. It is accepted for 60 points and 600 metres, a clean demonstration of uncommon but defensible recall.

segments.heading: Knowledge limits on Avatar and country names
segments.text: With little Avatar knowledge, the player falls back to Aang. Ghana is then chosen for the G-and-A country prompt. Both preserve the run, even though neither maximises rarity.

segments.heading: Last-second fallbacks for theme parks and literary devices
segments.text: Six Flags and irony each earn ten points. The player avoids a blank box, but the timing leaves almost no recovery margin; we would submit these safe answers a few seconds earlier.

segments.heading: Answer reveal and useful alternatives
segments.text: The review surfaces Ngram Viewer, Brazilian free-tailed bat, Guinea-Bissau, Legoland, and uncommon literary terms. Treat them as examples of retrieval routes, not a list guaranteed to solve another day's prompts.

takeaways: Keep a safe answer alive while looking for one quieter alternative.
Use specialist everyday knowledge such as buckwheat when the category fit is certain.
Submit a common answer before time expires when the subject is a genuine knowledge gap.
Read post-run alternatives to learn category routes, not to memorise a one-day solution list.
blocks.versionNote: The recording is a September 13, 2026 Sunday Wildcard Daily Dive. Prompts and response frequencies change, so the exact tiers are historical examples; the seven-prompt flow, timed input, feedback, and review behaviour are the parts to copy.
